narration: In 1962 a survey crew walked into a valley in Siberia and found four hundred hectares of pine lying flat, every trunk pointing outward from one empty clearing. Nothing stood. The centre was bare.
For sixty years the answer was a meteorite. Ask any geologist then and they would have told you to go and find the crater sitting under the moss. It had to be there. Everyone knew that.
Then they drilled it. No crater. No iron, and no shocked quartz anywhere in the soil column — which is the one thing a meteorite strike cannot fail to leave behind.
That absence should bother you. Whatever flattened that forest shares an orbit with us, and it never had to touch the ground to do what it did.

The object came apart in the air. Rock entering at fifteen kilometres a second compresses the air ahead of it until the pressure exceeds the strength of the stone, and the whole mass turns to heat and blast in under a second. Several kilometres up. Nothing lands.
So the crater was never missing. There was never going to be one. The flattened trees are the only evidence the event was ever going to leave behind.
